hints: First form the line through $A$ and $B$ using direction $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$.
Write this line as $\mathbf r=(1,2,-2)+\lambda(1,-3,3)$ and equate its components to those of $l$.
Solve any two of the three component equations for $\lambda$ and $\mu$.
Substitute those parameter values into the remaining component equation; its inconsistency proves that the lines do not intersect.
walkthrough:
Find the vector equation of the line passing through $A(1, 2, -2)$ and $B(2, -1, 1)$:
$$\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\mathbf{r}_{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$$

Write the vector equation of line $l$:
$$\mathbf{r}_l = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$$

Set up the system of component equations to test for intersection:
$$x: \quad 1 + \lambda = 1 + 2\mu \implies \lambda = 2\mu$$
$$y: \quad 2 - 3\lambda = -1 - 3\mu$$
$$z: \quad -2 + 3\lambda = 3 + 4\mu$$

Solve the $x$- and $y$-equations simultaneously for $\lambda$ and $\mu$:
Substitute $\lambda = 2\mu$ into the $y$-equation:
$$2 - 3(2\mu) = -1 - 3\mu$$
$$2 - 6\mu = -1 - 3\mu$$
$$3 = 3\mu \implies \mu = 1$$
$$\lambda = 2(1) = 2$$

Test consistency in the $z$-equation using $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = 1$:
$$\text{Left-hand side: } -2 + 3(2) = -2 + 6 = 4$$
$$\text{Right-hand side: } 3 + 4(1) = 3 + 4 = 7$$
Since $4 \neq 7$, the equations are contradictory.
Conclude that the two lines do not intersect.

ai_rubric.Testing Vector-Line Relationships: Forms the line through $A,B$. Derives $\mathbf r=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-2\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)$. For example the $j,k$ equations give $\lambda=-1$, $\mu=-2$, but then the $i$ components are $0\ne-3$.

hints: Let $P$ be a general point on $l$: $\mathbf p=(1,-1,3)+\mu(2,-3,4)$.
Form $\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf p-(1,2,-2)$; the foot occurs when this vector is perpendicular to the direction $(2,-3,4)$ of $l$.
Set $\overrightarrow{AP}\boldsymbol\cdot(2,-3,4)=0$ and solve the resulting linear equation for $\mu$.
Substitute that parameter back into the equation of $l$ to obtain the required position vector.
walkthrough:
Let $P$ be a general point on the line $l$ with parameter $\mu$:
$$\vec{OP} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2\mu \\ -1 - 3\mu \\ 3 + 4\mu \end{pmatrix}$$

Apply the perpendicularity condition $\vec{AP} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$ with the direction vector $\mathbf{d} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ of line $l$:
$$(2\mu)(2) + (-3 - 3\mu)(-3) + (5 + 4\mu)(4) = 0$$
$$4\mu + (9 + 9\mu) + (20 + 16\mu) = 0$$
$$29\mu + 29 = 0 \implies 29\mu = -29 \implies \mu = -1$$

Substitute $\mu = -1$ into $\vec{OP}$ to find the position vector of the foot of the perpendicular:
$$\vec{OP} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2(-1) \\ -1 - 3(-1) \\ 3 + 4(-1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - 2 \\ -1 + 3 \\ 3 - 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$$

ai_rubric.Perpendicular Projections in Vector Geom: For a general point $P$ on $l$, find $\vec{AP}$, e.g. $-3\mathbf j+5\mathbf k+\mu(2\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$; Derives $\mu=-1$; Concludes with $-\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-\mathbf k$.
